The sea potato Echinocardium cordatum initiates its life cycle as a minute free-swimming pluteus larva following external fertilisation. Following a period of planktotrophic feeding, the bipinnaria larva undergoes metamorphic climax and settles onto the seabed. At a sustained water temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], the time since birth at this larval-juvenile transition is approximately 39 days . This relatively brief planktonic duration, typical of many irregular echinoids, enables rapid colonisation of sandy substrates. Upon settlement, the newly metamorphosed juvenile possesses a wet weight at birth of just 0.00000088 grams [Wwb = 0.00000088 grams], a value that reflects the tiny egg diameter of roughly 119 micrometres from which it hatched. This minuscule initial mass imposes a severe energetic challenge, as the post-metamorphic individual must immediately commence deposit feeding on organic detritus and microbenthic algae to fuel its subsequent growth. The transition from the free-swimming larval stage to a burrowing existence is a critical bottleneck, with high early mortality reported in field populations.

Sexual maturation in Echinocardium cordatum is a protracted process, heavily modulated by ambient temperature. Within populations inhabiting temperate waters at 10 °C [T = 10 °C], individuals attain puberty at 1,095 days since birth [tp = 1,095 days since birth]. This three-year delay to the onset of gametogenesis is characteristic of a slow-paced life history strategy, where somatic growth is prioritised before the substantial energetic demands of reproductive tissue development. At the moment of reproductive activation, the typical individual has reached a test length at puberty of approximately 5.6 centimetres [Lp = approximately 5.6 centimetres] and a corresponding wet weight at puberty of 61.2 grams [Wwp = 61.2 grams]. This size threshold appears to be a robust predictor of gonad maturation across European populations. The sea potato's test, or body shell, continues to expand throughout the adult phase, ultimately reaching an ultimate test length of 9 centimetres [Li = 9 centimetres] in the oldest, largest specimens recovered during benthic surveys.

The energetic trajectory from puberty to maximum size reveals a substantial scope for continued somatic investment. The ultimate wet weight achieved by fully grown individuals is approximately 254 grams [Wwi = approximately 254 grams], a value that represents a more than fourfold increase from the mass recorded at the onset of sexual maturity. This considerable growth after puberty is sustained through the efficient processing of nutrient-poor sandy sediments. The relationship between test dimensions and mass yields an asymptotic body size that positions Echinocardium cordatum among the larger spatangoid burrowers in its ecological guild. In comparative terms, the ultimate wet weight of 254 grams [Wwi = 254 grams] is consistent with the upper size range documented for other members of the Loveniidae, though local food availability can significantly modulate the final mass attained. The species' capacity for continued growth well into the reproductive phase is a key life-history adaptation, allowing individuals to buffer against years of poor resource quality by maintaining high fecundity later in life.

Reproductive output in the sea potato is strongly tied to thermal conditions, with peak performance occurring in warmer waters. Under laboratory conditions simulating summer temperatures of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], females achieve their maximum reproductive rate, laying approximately 2,740 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 2,740 eggs per day]. This prodigious daily fecundity, sustained over several weeks of the spawning season, is fuelled by the extensive gonadal biomass supported by the large adult body size. The total annual fecundity can thus reach into the millions of eggs per individual, a broadcast-spawning strategy typical of echinoids that rely on chance encounters for gametic union. This high fecundity compensates for the extreme vulnerability of the minute, free-swimming pluteus larva and its negligible wet weight at birth of 0.00000088 grams [Wwb = 0.00000088 grams]. The stark mismatch between the infinitesimal mass of the propagule and the 254 gram [Wwi = 254 gram] ultimate wet weight of the adult underscores the enormous scope for growth inherent in the species' life cycle, a scope that demands sustained high feeding rates and favourable sedimentary conditions.

The complete lifespan of Echinocardium cordatum, documented from mark-recapture studies and growth-ring analysis of the test plates, extends to 20 years [am = 20 years] when individuals experience the stable thermal conditions of a 10 °C [T = 10 °C] environment. This longevity is remarkable among burrowing echinoids and reflects a slow senescence rate combined with low natural predation pressure once the animal reaches a refuge depth within the sediment. Over this extended period, the sea potato must navigate numerous ecological challenges, including seasonal food shortages and physical disturbance from storms. By spreading reproductive output across many years and achieving an ultimate test length of 9 centimetres [Li = 9 centimetres], Echinocardium cordatum maximises its fitness in the unpredictable, low-productivity sandy habitats it occupies across the Northeast Atlantic and Mediterranean Sea.
